title: Below the Line
passages:
The Marrow groaned as the wave caught her beam-on, rail burying until green water washed the deck. Sol didn't wait for the roll-back. She was already moving, one hand on the shrouds, the other snatching the coiled heaving-line from the pinrail where it lived for exactly this. Nia beat her to the boat-hook, aluminum shaft warm from the sun they'd had at noon, and didn't ask what to do — just ran the hook out over the stanchion, braced her boots on the wet nonskid, and waited for the next wallow to bring the water up to them.

"There — starboard quarter, twenty meters!" Wren's voice cracked over the deck speaker, thin with cold and the wind stealing words. She stood frozen at the winch, slate dark in her hand, the drum silent behind her.

Sol didn't look up. "Got him. Nia, hook the collar. I'll take the line."

The boat-hook dipped, caught, missed, caught again on the second roll — the orange webbing of Dey's harness, torn loose from its tether. Nia's arms locked, shoulders hiked to her ears, hauling dead weight through water that didn't want to give him up. Sol took the line two-handed, walking it back hand-over-hand, boots sliding on the deck's cant. The Marrow heaved the other way, rail lifting, and the water rushed off like a flushed tank, leaving Dey dangling in the hook's grip, half-in half-out, a seal pup caught in a net.

"Steady!" Sol barked, and Nia planted herself, muscles jumping under her soaked jacket.

They swung him inboard together on the next roll, a graceless tangle of limbs and rope, and dropped him on the nonskid like a sack of wet cement. Dey didn't gasp. Didn't cough. His lips were the gray of old ash, eyes open but fixed on nothing, pupils blown wide against the dim. Water bubbled at the corner of his mouth, thin and slow. His chest moved — barely — a reflex the deep hadn't finished killing yet.

"Dey." Sol dropped beside him, fingers finding carotid, wrist, the soft place under the jaw. Pulse thready, skin cold as the bilge. "Dey, look at me."

His eyes didn't shift. Didn't blink. The storm screamed in the rigging and the Marrow took another hit, but the man on the deck didn't flinch, didn't shrink, didn't do anything a living body should do when the world tries to shake it apart.

Nia crouched on his other side, face pale in the running lights, one hand hovering over his chest like she wanted to press down and couldn't decide where. "He's heavy," she said, quiet. "Too heavy. Like the water's still in him."

Sol's jaw tightened. She peeled back Dey's eyelid with a thumb, watched the pupil stay round and dead. "The deep doesn't let go easy. Wren — get the slate. Now."

Wren didn't move. The winch drum sat silent behind her, the slack line coiling in the scuppers like a dead snake. Her slate glowed faint in her hand, the same eleven seconds she'd found in her own record blinking steady at the top of the build.

"Wren!" Sol's voice cracked the wind. "The slate. His slate. Read it."

Wren came off the winch like something had cut her loose.

She dropped to her knees on the wet nonskid, took Dey's collar in both hands, and thumbed the housing clip on the slate puck — a gray disc the size of a saucer, strapped where a diver's throat meets the harness, writing down depth and air and pulse whether the diver likes it or not. Her fingers found the gasket, found water beaded in the seam, and she swore once, softly, at the water.

"Talk while you work," Sol said.

"This is my talking face."

She seated the puck in the cradle on her own slate, the little dock that pulls a diver's record out and lays it flat, and the screen filled with a green ladder of numbers. Behind her the drum sat dead, its slack line slithering in the scuppers with every roll.

"Fourteen fifty-two, he's on the rail," Wren said. "No loop, no scrubber, no canister on his chest to take the carbon dioxide back out of his breath. One lungful and a bad idea. He's at forty-one meters by fifteen-oh-four, which is faster than I go with a rig and air." She stopped. "He was trying to get somewhere before something happened."

"What happened," Nia said.

"That's the problem." Wren dragged the timeline open with her thumb. "The slate kept writing the whole way down. Depth, air, heart rate, fifty-one minutes of it. There's just nothing underneath the numbers. No sound, no picture, no voice. Not corrupted. Not jammed. *Empty.*"

Sol's hand was still on Dey's jaw, holding his head out of the roll. "Meaning what."

"Meaning below thirty meters he stopped laying anything down." Wren looked up, rain running into her collar. "You know the line. Thirty meters, give or take. Under it the deep doesn't hurt you, it just stops filing. Whatever you did down there never gets written, so there's nothing for me to rebuild. I don't lose an hour and hand it back. I can't find it to begin with. Nobody comes up from under the line with the hour still on them."

"So he gets out of his debt for free," Nia said. She had Dey's wrist between two fingers, counting, her face doing nothing at all. "Forty-one meters. That's the pocket, isn't it. That's Rusk's pharmacy."

"He got there," Wren said. "And it took the rest."

"Then don't tell me what's missing." Sol sat back on her heels. "Tell me it's a cut."

That was the thing Wren did. A cut left a seam — so she ran the seam check without being asked, laying Dey's record against every other clock on the boat that had watched the same hour: the inclinometer in the masthead, the deck camera's counter, the drum's encoder up on the winch housing. Two clocks that disagree by half a second mean a hand was in there with a blade. Two clocks that agree and leave the middle blank mean nobody touched it.

The check came back in four seconds. Every clock on the Marrow agreed. The middle was blank.

"Water," she said. "It's water. Nothing was edited."

She heard herself say it and felt the floor of her stomach go, because she had run this same check last night on a different slate and gotten the other answer.

Dey's mouth moved. His eyes stayed fixed on the rain, but his jaw worked, and what came out was not a word a half-drowned man should have breath for.

"Wren."

Nia's counting fingers stopped. "That's twice now."

On the console above them the backup channel — the emergency band, the one that carries four hundred meters and no further — opened with a hiss, and the man at forty-two meters said her name again, patient as a man reading off a list.

Wren killed the deck speaker with the back of her hand, but the name hung there anyway, the way a struck bell hangs.

"He knows me," she said.

"Everybody knows the tech," Nia said, not looking up from Dey's wrist. "You're the one who talks to the dead men's slates."

"I've never given a diver my name. I've never met a man at forty-two meters." Wren's thumb was already moving, pulling last night's traffic up out of the console. "And I've got a worse problem, which is that I know his."

She let it play.

The recording came thin under the storm-static, but the voice on it was hers — flat and winded, the way she sounded when she was working. *At pocket. Seal intact. I see it.* A pause, her own breathing loud in the mic. Then smaller, turned away from the boat, toward someone: *I'll bring the winch. I swear it.*

Nobody said anything. The water ran off the deck, and Dey's chest went up and came down.

"That's last night," Sol said finally. "You slept in the chair last night. I watched you."

"I don't remember recording it." Wren set the slate on the nonskid, carefully, like it might go off. "There's a fifty-two-minute hole in my own deck log. Sealed shut by my own hand, in my own method. I went down there. I came back up. And then I cut the whole thing out of myself, and I don't remember doing that either."

Sol's face didn't move, but her grip on Dey's jaw did.

"Then that settles it," she said. "Nobody goes near that tower. We ride it out, we—"

"Ride it out on what." Nia said it flat, the way you'd read a gauge. "Rusk is back at first light for the case or the boat. Teo has one cartridge left after what Rusk pocketed. There's no tomorrow to ride into."

Sol's mouth shut.

"The pocket's the only score in four hundred meters," Wren said. "Sealed pharmacy, forty-two meters, dry as a bone. It's why Dey went. It's why Rusk dangled it. One pull of that and we buy the berths and pay the debt and keep the Marrow." She was already doing the sum and hating the answer. "But somebody has to bring it up. And here's the part nobody wants."

She crossed to the rig locker, spun the dogs, and hauled it open on three dive suits hanging orange and scarred, their umbilicals coiled at the collars — the hoses that carry air down and a voice back up. She put her hand flat on the first chest seal.

"Thirty-meter rating. This one too. This one." She slapped each in turn. "Past thirty the seal creeps. You take water into the suit at forty-two and it's not a rescue, it's a dredge." She looked at Sol. "There's one suit on this boat rated to forty-two. It's mine. So it's me or it's nobody, and nobody leaves a girl's brother to die for arithmetic."

"There's a cost," Sol said quietly. "You know the line. You go under thirty, you come up missing the swim. Like Dey. Like me."

"I know." Wren pulled her own suit off its hook, the deep-rated one, heavier than the rest. "I did it last night and I'm still missing it. So I'll do it again, and lose this one too, and somebody topside is going to have to explain to me why we're all crying when I break the surface."

She sat on the deck coaming and shoved her legs in. Behind her the drum sat dead with one good pull left in it, and every soul on deck knew it, and nobody said it.

"I'm going down," she said. "Keep the channel open. If he says my name again, write down what else he says."
